Battle of Normandy. The Battle of Normandy was the largest amphibious invasion in history, codenamed Operation Overlord. It took place from June to August 1944 as over one hundred fifty thousand Allied troops stormed the beaches of Normandy, France, to establish a foothold in Nazi-occupied Western Europe. Led by American General Dwight D. Eisenhower, the assault broke through German defensive lines and opened a decisive western front. The battle's success and the subsequent breakout into France turned the tide of the war in Europe and began the liberation of occupied Western Europe.

This was planned as the primary Allied assault to break German control of Western Europe, defended by Hitler's Atlantic Wall fortifications. Supreme Commander Dwight D. Eisenhower coordinated American, British, and Canadian forces, with Field Marshal Bernard Montgomery commanding ground forces. German General Erwin Rommel had reinforced Normandy's defenses, but Hitler refused to move panzer reserves without direct orders, paralyzing German response.

On D-Day, June 6, 1944, five thousand ships and over one hundred fifty thousand troops landed on five beach sectors named Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno, and Sword across a fifty-mile front. American forces faced the fiercest resistance at Omaha Beach, while British and Canadian landings were more successful. Airborne drops behind German lines by American 101st and 82nd Airborne divisions and British 6th Airborne disrupted German reinforcements and secured critical objectives.

The beachhead expanded slowly through hedgerow combat in the Norman bocage, dense and tangled countryside, with breakout delayed by German resistance and poor weather. American forces captured Saint-Lô and Cherbourg, while British and Canadian forces pushed toward Caen, delayed by German panzer counterattacks. The Falaise Pocket in mid-August trapped and destroyed a German army group, breaking German resistance. The Allies liberated Paris and advanced toward Germany. Normandy stands as the Allies' defining offensive of World War II, the moment industrial-scale amphibious assault proved feasible and strategic surprise and coordination could overcome a prepared enemy.
